title: Supercharge Your Classroom Management Plan With Detailed Modeling plan-through-modeling/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains how ordinary modeling -- demonstrating a task in front of the class -- can be made dramatically more effective by adding a single element: explicit, realistic detail. Rather than performing a task generically at the front of the room, he recommends teachers act it out at a student's desk, surrounded by students, including peripheral steps like clearing space or lining up for materials, and even acting out common misbehaviors and what happens as a result. He argues this peripheral, often-overlooked detail matters more than modeling the task itself, because it eliminates ambiguity, gives students a clear picture of expectations, and does so in an engaging, participatory way. Using the specific example of teaching students not to call out in class, he describes role-playing exercises where a student plays teacher while the real teacher demonstrates the rudeness of interrupting, and where volunteers act out breaking rules so the whole class can watch consequences delivered step by step. He contends that merely explaining classroom rules is only minimally effective compared to students actively experiencing what breaking a rule looks and feels like, and closes by calling detailed modeling one of the single most effective tools available for communicating expectations.
points: Adding explicit, realistic detail to ordinary modeling -- rather than performing a task generically at the front of the room -- significantly increases its effectiveness.
The 'peripheral' steps of a task (e.g., clearing a desk, lining up for materials) are often the most overlooked but most important parts to model in detail.
Detailed modeling should extend to misbehavior itself: acting out common rule violations, such as calling out, and demonstrating exactly what consequence follows.
Merely explaining classroom rules is described as only minimally effective compared to students actively experiencing, through role-play, what breaking a rule looks like.
Detailed modeling is framed as fun and participatory for students while also making expectations unambiguous, reducing later rule violations.
quotes: Modeling is so effective that it should be among your most often used teaching strategies.
However, you can supercharge the effectiveness of what you’re modeling, regardless of what it is, by adding an important element: explicit detail.
It’s the peripheral stuff–the stuff that teachers typically don’t model–that is the most important and will make the greatest difference to your teaching.
Students’ knowing what is expected of them is a critical part of any successful classroom management plan, and detailed modeling does just that. Too many teachers are vague in this regard.

To model calling out, the teacher might sit at a student’s desk while a student plays the part of the teacher. This gives the teacher the opportunity to demonstrate the rudeness, and even absurdity, of interrupting someone who is speaking.
Merely explaining classroom rules, or anything else for that matter, is minimally effective. Students must actively participate in and experience what it means to break rules.
Nothing is as effective as detailed modeling in communicating anything important to your students… nothing.
